summary.text: Choose an explicit very slowly divergent $f$, defined from finite hitting-set bounds for short odd cycles, so that the profile bound forces deletion of at most $i$ edges at scale $i$ to eliminate all odd cycles up to a rapidly growing length. Iterating these deletions leaves only small sets of affected endpoints, and a multiscale layering-and-gluing argument yields a 3-coloring of every finite graph satisfying the bound; compactness would turn any infinite-chromatic example into a finite non-3-colorable induced subgraph, a contradiction.

full_proof.text:
We disprove the assertion by constructing one particular function \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) with \(f(n)\to\infty\) for which the asserted graph cannot exist. In fact, for this function every finite graph satisfying the required edge-deletion profile is 3-colorable. A compactness argument then rules out an infinite-chromatic graph with that profile.

Throughout, for a finite-vertex subgraph \(A\) let
\[
  \delta(A)=\min\{|E|:E\subseteq E(A)\text{ and }A-E\text{ is bipartite}\}.
\]
For an arbitrary graph \(G\), put
\[
  p_G(n)=\max\{\delta(A):A\text{ is a finite subgraph of }G,
                    \ |V(A)|=n\}.
\]
If there is no such subgraph, its contribution is harmless and may be taken as zero. The conjectured inequality is exactly \(p_G(n)\le f(n)\) for every \(n\).

We shall repeatedly use two elementary facts about this profile.

First, if \(H\) embeds injectively into \(G\), then
\[
  p_H(n)\le p_G(n)\qquad(n\in\mathbb N).
\]
Indeed, map an \(n\)-vertex subgraph of \(H\) into \(G\), choose a minimum bipartizing edge set there, and pull that edge set and a bipartition back through the injection. Injectivity ensures that the number of pulled-back edges does not increase. In particular, the profile inequality passes to all subgraphs and induced subgraphs.

Second, if \(\delta(A)\le r\), then \(A\) is \((r+2)\)-colorable. To see this, choose a set \(E\) of at most \(r\) edges such that \(A-E\) is bipartite. Choose one endpoint from each edge in \(E\), give these chosen vertices separate colors, and use two further colors for a bipartition of all remaining vertices. Every deleted edge has at least one chosen endpoint, so this is proper. Consequently, if \(p_G(n)\le r\) uniformly in \(n\), then every finite induced subgraph of \(G\) is \((r+2)\)-colorable, and hence so is \(G\).

The last implication is the standard coloring compactness theorem. For completeness, for fixed \(k\), consider the compact product \(\{1,\dots,k\}^{V(G)}\). For every edge \(uv\), the condition that the two coordinates at \(u,v\) differ is closed. Any finite collection of these conditions involves only finitely many vertices and is satisfiable if every finite induced subgraph is \(k\)-colorable. The finite-intersection property therefore gives a point satisfying all edge conditions, namely a \(k\)-coloring of \(G\). In particular, a graph of infinite chromatic number has, for every finite \(k\), a finite induced subgraph which is not \(k\)-colorable.

We next develop the quantitative ingredients used to define the counterexample function.

----------------------------------------------------------------
1. A bounded hitting-witness construction
----------------------------------------------------------------

For integers \(L,d\ge0\), define recursively
\[
 B(L,0)=0,\qquad B(L,d+1)=L\bigl(B(L,d)+1\bigr).
\]
We need the following finite combinatorial lemma.

**Hitting-witness lemma.** Let \(\mathcal P\) be a family of finite subsets of some set, each of cardinality at most \(L\). Suppose that for every finite set \(t\) with \(|t|<d\), there is a member \(q\in\mathcal P\) disjoint from \(t\). Then there is a finite set \(W\), with
\[
 |W|\le B(L,d),
\]
such that for every \(t\) with \(|t|<d\), some \(q\in\mathcal P\) satisfies
\[
 q\subseteq W\quad\text{and}\quad q\cap t=\varnothing.
\]

Proof is by induction on \(d\). For \(d=0\), take \(W=\varnothing\); there is no set \(t\) of size less than zero. For \(d+1\), first choose \(s\in\mathcal P\) disjoint from the empty set, so \(|s|\le L\). For every \(e\in s\), apply the induction hypothesis to the family
\[
 \mathcal P_e=\{q\in\mathcal P:e\notin q\}.
\]
This family has the required avoidance property at level \(d\): if \(|t|<d\), apply the original hypothesis to \(t\cup\{e\}\), whose size is at most \(d\), obtaining a member disjoint from both \(t\) and \(e\). Thus there is a set \(W_e\) of size at most \(B(L,d)\) supporting all the required avoiders in \(\mathcal P_e\). Set
\[
 W=s\cup\bigcup_{e\in s}W_e.
\]
Then
\[
 |W|\le |s|+|s|B(L,d)
      \le L(B(L,d)+1)=B(L,d+1).
\]
Given \(t\) with \(|t|<d+1\), if \(s\cap t=\varnothing\), use \(s\). Otherwise choose \(e\in s\cap t\). The set \(t\setminus\{e\}\) has size less than \(d\), so \(W_e\) contains a member \(q\in\mathcal P_e\) disjoint from \(t\setminus\{e\}\). Since \(e\notin q\), it is disjoint from all of \(t\). This proves the lemma.

Apply this to edge sets. Suppose that in a graph \(G\), for every set \(t\) of fewer than \(d\) edges there is an edge set \(q\) such that
\[
 |q|\le L,\qquad q\subseteq E(G),\qquad
 (V(q),q)\text{ is nonbipartite},\qquad q\cap t=\varnothing.
\]
The hitting-witness lemma gives a set \(W\) of at most \(B(L,d)\) edges which contains a suitable \(q\) avoiding every \(t\) of fewer than \(d\) edges. Form the finite subgraph \(A\) whose edge set is \(W\) and whose vertices are the endpoints of edges in \(W\). Then
\[
 |V(A)|\le 2B(L,d).
\]
No set of fewer than \(d\) edges can make \(A\) bipartite: if \(t\) did, choose \(q\subseteq W\) disjoint from \(t\) as above. A bipartition of \(A-t\) would restrict to a bipartition of the graph with edge set \(q\), contrary to the choice of \(q\). Hence
\[
 \delta(A)\ge d.
\]
We have proved the useful profile consequence
\[
 \boxed{\text{Under the preceding robust-obstruction hypothesis, there is }
 n\le2B(L,d)\text{ with }p_G(n)\ge d.} \tag{1}
\]

----------------------------------------------------------------
2. Deleting a few edges eliminates all short odd closed walks
----------------------------------------------------------------

Call an odd closed walk of length at most \(L\) a short odd loop at scale \(L\). If a graph contains such a walk \(P\), the set \(q\) of distinct edges traversed by \(P\) has size at most \(L\), and the graph with edge set \(q\) is nonbipartite: a bipartition would force every closed walk to have even length.

It follows from (1) that if
\[
 p_G(n)<d\qquad\text{for every }n\le2B(L,d), \tag{2}
\]
then one can delete fewer than \(d\) edges from \(G\) so that the remaining graph has no odd closed walk of length at most \(L\).

Indeed, suppose this were impossible. Then, after deleting any set \(t\) of fewer than \(d\) edges, the remaining graph would contain an odd closed walk of length at most \(L\). Its distinct edge set \(q\) would have size at most \(L\), would be disjoint from \(t\), and would span a nonbipartite graph. Thus the robust-obstruction hypothesis of (1) would hold, giving some \(n\le2B(L,d)\) with \(p_G(n)\ge d\), contradicting (2).

For later reference, write
\[
 \operatorname{OddFree}(G,L)

after the assertion that every odd closed walk in \(G\) has length strictly greater than \(L\).

We also record two standard quantitative walk facts.

**Finite-root walk bound.** Suppose \(S\) is a finite set in a graph \(G\), and every vertex is joined by a walk of length at most \(R\) to some member of \(S\). Then any two vertices in the same component can be joined by a walk of length at most
\[
 D=(2R+1)|S|+2R. \tag{3}
\]
To prove this, choose for each vertex a root in \(S\) and a walk of length at most \(R\) to that root. Make an auxiliary graph on \(S\), joining two distinct roots when they can be joined in \(G\) by a walk of length at most \(2R+1\). The endpoints of every edge of \(G\) have either the same root or adjacent roots in the auxiliary graph. Thus a walk in \(G\) projects to connectivity in the auxiliary graph. Two connected roots can be joined there by a simple path with at most \(|S|\) edges. Lift each auxiliary edge at cost at most \(2R+1\), and add the two root walks, at total cost at most (3).

**Short odd loop from bounded components.** If every pair of connected vertices of \(G\) can be joined by a walk of length at most \(D\), and \(G\) is not bipartite, then \(G\) has an odd closed walk of length at most
\[
 2D+1. \tag{4}
\]
Choose one root in each component and color a vertex by the parity of its distance from the root. Since the graph is not bipartite, some edge \(uv\) has endpoints of the same parity. Shortest root-to-\(u\) and root-to-\(v\) paths both have length at most \(D\). Traversing the first, then \(uv\), then the reverse of the second produces an odd closed walk of length at most \(2D+1\).

A useful special case is that a nonbipartite graph on \(m\) vertices has an odd closed walk of length at most \(2m+1\). Consequently,
\[
 \operatorname{OddFree}(G,L),\quad 2|V(G)|+1\le L
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad G\text{ is bipartite}. \tag{5}
\]
The same applies to every finite induced subgraph, because an odd closed walk in an induced subgraph is also one in the original graph.

----------------------------------------------------------------
3. The scales and the slowly growing budget
----------------------------------------------------------------

Define
\[
 R_i=4i(i+2)
\]
and
\[
 L_i=
 2\bigl((2R_{i+1}+1)i(i+1)+2R_{i+1}\bigr)
 +4(i+1)+10. \tag{6}
\]
Finally define the threshold
\[
 T_i=2B(L_i,i+1)+i. \tag{7}
\]
For every \(n\), let
\[
 f(n)=\min\{i:n\le T_i\}. \tag{8}
\]
This minimum exists, since \(T_n\ge n\).

This function tends to infinity, although it need not be monotone. Fix \(b\). If \(f(n)<b\), then by (8)
\[
 n\le T_{f(n)}\le \sum_{i<b}T_i.
\]
Therefore every
\[
 n>\sum_{i<b}T_i

automatically satisfies \(f(n)\ge b\). Thus \(f(n)\to\infty\).

The crucial feature of this definition is
\[
 n\le2B(L_i,i+1)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f(n)\le i, \tag{9}
\]
because then \(n\le T_i\), so \(i\) is one of the candidates in the minimum (8).

----------------------------------------------------------------
4. A sparse three-coloring lemma
----------------------------------------------------------------

We shall use colors \(0,1,2\), with color \(2\) regarded as exceptional.

Suppose \(G,H\) are graphs on the same vertex set, \(H\) is bipartite, and \(S\) is a set such that every edge of \(G\) either is an edge of \(H\), or has both endpoints in \(S\). If the induced graph \(G[S]\) is also bipartite, then \(G\) has a 3-coloring in which every vertex receiving color \(2\) lies in \(S\).

Indeed, fix a bipartition of \(H\), and a bipartition \(S=S_0\sqcup S_1\) of \(G[S]\). Give every vertex in \(S_0\) color \(2\), and every other vertex its \(H\)-color \(0\) or \(1\). There is no edge with both endpoints in \(S_0\). If a \(G\)-edge is in \(H\), then either it retains the two different \(H\)-colors, or one endpoint has changed to color \(2\). If it is not in \(H\), both endpoints lie in \(S\); because it crosses \(S_0,S_1\), exactly one endpoint is in \(S_0\), and hence its endpoint colors differ. This proves the claim.

We also require an explicit way of gluing two 3-colorings across distance layers. Let \(h:V(G)\to\mathbb N\) satisfy
\[
 |h(u)-h(v)|\le1\quad\text{on every edge }uv. \tag{10}
\]
Suppose a coloring \(a\) is proper on edges whose endpoints have height at most \(t+2\), and a coloring \(b\) is proper on edges whose endpoints have height at least \(t\). Suppose moreover that
\[
 a(v)\ne2\quad(t\le h(v)\le t+2),
\]
\[
 b(v)\ne2\quad(t\le h(v)\le t+3).
\]
Then the two colorings can be glued to a proper 3-coloring \(c\), and it may be done so that
\[
 c(v)=2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad h(v)\le t+2\text{ or }b(v)=2. \tag{11}
\]

Here is the explicit construction. Put \(c=a\) on \(h\le t\), and \(c=b\) on \(h\ge t+3\). At height \(t+1\), put
\[
 c(v)=
 \begin{cases}
 b(v),&a(v)=b(v),\\
 2,&a(v)\ne b(v),\ b(v)=0,\\
 0,&a(v)\ne b(v),\ b(v)=1,
 \end{cases}

after noting that in this layer both \(a(v)\) and \(b(v)\) lie in \(\{0,1\}\). At height \(t+2\), put
\[
 c(v)=
 \begin{cases}
 b(v),&a(v)=b(v),\\
 2,&a(v)\ne b(v),\ b(v)=0,\\
 1,&a(v)\ne b(v),\ b(v)=1.
 \end{cases}

after the same observation. Condition (10) means an edge can meet only equal or consecutive layers. On layers at most \(t\), properness follows from \(a\), and on layers at least \(t+3\), from \(b\). For the remaining possibilities—two vertices in layer \(t+1\), two in layer \(t+2\), or endpoints in consecutive pairs \((t,t+1)\), \((t+1,t+2)\), \((t+2,t+3)\)—substitution in the displayed rules shows that equality of the new colors would force equality of the relevant old \(a\)-colors or old \(b\)-colors. That contradicts the assumed properness. The asymmetric choices \(0\) at layer \(t+1\) and \(1\) at layer \(t+2\) are precisely what prevents a clash across the middle pair of layers. This checks properness, and the formulas immediately imply (11).

Finally, if a finite set \(X\) has size at most \(m\), then among the \(m+1\) disjoint four-layer intervals
\[
 [q+4j+1,q+4j+4],\qquad 0\le j\le m,

there is one containing no vertex of \(X\). Otherwise, selecting one point of \(X\) from each interval would give \(m+1\) distinct points in \(X\).

----------------------------------------------------------------
5. The multiscale coloring lemma
----------------------------------------------------------------

We now prove the central induction.

Let
\[
 G_0\supseteq G_1\supseteq\cdots\supseteq G_n

a sequence of graphs on the same vertex set. Suppose there are sets \(S_i\), for \(0\le i<n\), such that
\[
 |S_i|\le2(i+1), \tag{12}
\]
and every edge of \(G_i\) either remains in \(G_{i+1}\), or has both endpoints in \(S_i\). Assume also
\[
 \operatorname{OddFree}(G_i,L_i)\qquad(0\le i<n), \tag{13}
\]
and that \(G_n\) is bipartite.

Put
\[
 A_n=S_0\cup\cdots\cup S_{n-1},\qquad A_0=\varnothing.

equation (12) gives
\[
 |A_n|\le\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}2(i+1)=n(n+1). \tag{14}
\]
We claim that \(G_0\) has a 3-coloring \(c\) such that every vertex of color \(2\) can be reached in \(G_0\), by a walk of length at most \(R_n\), from a vertex of \(A_n\). 

We prove this by induction on \(n\). For \(n=0\), \(G_0\) is bipartite, so use only colors \(0,1\); the assertion about color \(2\) is vacuous.

Assume the result for \(n\), and consider a sequence ending at \(G_{n+1}\). Let \(A=A_n\), and put \(R=R_{n+1}\). Define a truncated distance from \(A\) by
\[
 h(v)=\min\bigl(R+1,\operatorname{dist}_{G_0}(A,v)\bigr),

taking the second quantity to be infinite when there is no such walk. More explicitly, \(h(v)\) is the least member of the set consisting of \(R+1\) and all lengths of walks in \(G_0\) from a point of \(A\) to \(v\). Then:

* \(h=0\) on \(A\);
* \(|h(u)-h(v)|\le1\) for every edge \(uv\) of \(G_0\);
* if \(h(v)\le R\), there is a walk from \(A\) to \(v\) of length exactly \(h(v)\), all of whose vertices have height at most \(R\).

Let
\[
 X=\{v:h(v)\le R\}.

after iterating the edge-agreement hypothesis, every edge of \(G_0\) either belongs to \(G_n\), or has both endpoints in \(A\). Consider the witnessing \(G_0\)-walk from \(A\) to a vertex \(v\in X\). Delete from its beginning everything up to and including its last edge which is not in \(G_n\). If there is no such edge, retain the whole walk. The remaining suffix is a \(G_n[X]\)-walk to \(v\), starts at a vertex of \(A\), and has length at most \(R\). Thus every vertex of \(G_n[X]\) is within distance \(R\) of
\[
 A'=A\cap X,

and by (14), \(|A'|\le n(n+1)\).

We claim that \(G_n[X]\) is bipartite. If not, the finite-root bound (3) says that any two connected vertices can be joined by a walk of length at most
\[
 D=(2R+1)|A'|+2R
  \le(2R+1)n(n+1)+2R.
\]
By (4), \(G_n[X]\), and hence \(G_n\), would contain an odd closed walk of length at most
\[
 2\bigl((2R+1)n(n+1)+2R\bigr)+1.
\]
By definition (6), this is strictly less than \(L_n\), contradicting \(\operatorname{OddFree}(G_n,L_n)\). Hence \(G_n[X]\) is bipartite.

Apply the induction hypothesis inside \(X\) to
\[
 G_0[X]\supseteq G_1[X]\supseteq\cdots\supseteq G_n[X].

the odd-loop conditions pass to induced subgraphs, and the restricted sets \(S_i\cap X\) retain the bounds (12). We obtain an inner 3-coloring \(a\) of \(G_0[X]\) whose color-2 vertices are within \(G_0[X]\)-distance at most \(R_n\) from \(A\cap X\). Since \(h=0\) on \(A\) and height changes by at most one along an edge, every such exceptional vertex satisfies
\[
 a(v)=2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad h(v)\le R_n. \tag{15}
\]

We next construct an outer coloring. The induced graph \(G_n[S_n]\) is bipartite. Indeed, if it were not, by (5) it would contain an odd closed walk of length at most
\[
 2|S_n|+1\le4(n+1)+1<L_n,

again contradicting \(\operatorname{OddFree}(G_n,L_n)\). The graph \(G_{n+1}\) is bipartite, and every edge of \(G_n\) either lies in \(G_{n+1}\) or has both endpoints in \(S_n\). The sparse-coloring lemma therefore gives a 3-coloring \(b\) of \(G_n\) such that
\[
 \{v:b(v)=2\}\subseteq S_n,
 \qquad |\{v:b(v)=2\}|\le2(n+1). \tag{16}
\]

Use the empty-four-layer observation with \(q=R_n\), \(m=2(n+1)\), and the exceptional set in (16). We obtain an integer \(j\), with \(0\le j\le2(n+1)\), such that no vertex colored \(2\) by \(b\) has height in
\[
 [R_n+4j+1,R_n+4j+4].
\]
Set
\[
 t=R_n+4j+1.

the scale identity
\[
 R_{n+1}=R_n+4\bigl(2(n+1)\bigr)+4

after direct expansion of \(R_i=4i(i+2)\), ensures that \(t+3\le R\). Thus the inner coloring is available through height \(t+2\). By (15), it uses no color \(2\) in layers \(t,t+1,t+2\). The outer coloring uses no color \(2\) in layers \(t,t+1,t+2,t+3\).

The inner coloring is proper for \(G_0\)-edges with both endpoints below height \(t+2\). The outer coloring is also proper for every \(G_0\)-edge with both endpoints of height at least \(t\): such an edge either is in \(G_n\), where \(b\) is proper, or both endpoints lie in \(A\), where their heights are zero; the latter alternative is impossible because \(t\ge1\). We may therefore apply the explicit gluing construction of the preceding section. It produces a 3-coloring \(c\) of \(G_0\) such that a color-2 vertex either has height at most \(t+2\), or is color \(2\) under \(b\).

In the first case, \(t+2\le R\), so the defining property of the truncated height gives a walk of length at most \(R=R_{n+1}\) from a vertex of \(A\) to \(v\). In the second case, (16) gives \(v\in S_n\), and the length-zero walk starts at \(v\). In either case the starting point belongs to
\[
 A\cup S_n=A_{n+1}.

This completes the induction and proves the multiscale coloring lemma.

----------------------------------------------------------------
6. Every finite graph with profile bounded by \(f\) is 3-colorable
----------------------------------------------------------------

Let \(G\) be a finite graph satisfying
\[
 p_G(n)\le f(n)\qquad\text{for every }n. \tag{17}
\]
The same inequality holds for every subgraph \(H\subseteq G\).

Fix \(i\ge0\) and such an \(H\). If
\[
 n\le2B(L_i,i+1),

then by (17) and (9),
\[
 p_H(n)\le p_G(n)\le f(n)\le i<i+1.

the short-odd-loop deletion result from Section 2, with \(L=L_i\) and \(d=i+1\), therefore provides a set of at most \(i\) edges whose deletion from \(H\) leaves a graph satisfying \(\operatorname{OddFree}(-,L_i)\).

We now recursively construct graphs
\[
 G=G_0\supseteq G_1\supseteq G_2\supseteq\cdots.

after \(G_i\) has been constructed, apply the preceding conclusion to \(H=G_i\) and index \(i+1\). Choose a set \(E_i\) of at most \(i+1\) edges such that
\[
 G_{i+1}=G_i-E_i
 \quad\text{satisfies}\quad
 \operatorname{OddFree}(G_{i+1},L_{i+1}). \tag{18}
\]
For index zero the corresponding deletion set has size zero, so already
\[
 \operatorname{OddFree}(G_0,L_0). \tag{19}
\]
Let \(S_i\) be the set of endpoints of edges in \(E_i\). Then
\[
 |S_i|\le2(i+1), \tag{20}
\]
and every edge of \(G_i\) either remains in \(G_{i+1}\), or has both endpoints in \(S_i\). Thus (18)--(20) give exactly the hypotheses required by the multiscale lemma, except that we must stop at a bipartite member of the sequence.

Let
\[
 N=2|V(G)|+1.

the graph \(G_N\) satisfies \(\operatorname{OddFree}(G_N,L_N)\). The explicit expression (6) certainly gives
\[
 L_N\ge2|V(G)|+1.

Since \(G_N\) has at most \(|V(G)|\) vertices, (5) shows that \(G_N\) is bipartite. Apply the multiscale lemma to
\[
 G_0,\ldots,G_N.

It yields a 3-coloring of \(G_0=G\). We have proved:

\[
 \boxed{\text{Every finite graph }G\text{ satisfying }p_G(n)\le f(n)
 \text{ for all }n\text{ is 3-colorable}.} \tag{21}
\]

----------------------------------------------------------------
7. Contradiction with the conjecture
----------------------------------------------------------------

For clarity, we finally explain the finite-witness reduction that applies (21) to the statement in the question, including the minor issue that the chosen function \(f\) is not monotone.

For any divergent function \(g:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\), define its tail minimum
\[
 \underline g(n)=\min_{m\ge n}g(m).

the function \(\underline g\) is nondecreasing, satisfies \(\underline g(n)\le g(n)\), and still tends to infinity. The last assertion follows because, given \(b\), eventually every value of \(g\) is at least \(b\), so the minimum over every sufficiently late tail is at least \(b\).

Suppose the conjecture were true. Apply it to \(\underline f\). We obtain a graph \(X\) of infinite chromatic number such that
\[
 p_X(n)\le\underline f(n)\qquad(n\in\mathbb N). \tag{22}

the coloring compactness theorem gives a finite induced subgraph \(F\) of \(X\) which is not 3-colorable (indeed, one may choose one which is not 4-colorable). Profile bounds pass to induced subgraphs, so
\[
 p_F(n)\le p_X(n)\le\underline f(n)\le f(n)

everywhere. Relabeling the finite vertex set, if desired, does not change either colorability or any of the quantities \(p_F(n)\). Thus \(F\) is a finite graph satisfying the hypothesis of (21). It must therefore be 3-colorable, a contradiction.

Hence the conjectured universal statement is false. Explicitly, the divergent function defined by (6)--(8),
\[
 f(n)=\min\left\{i:
 n\le 2B(L_i,i+1)+i\right\},
\]
where
\[
 B(L,0)=0,\qquad B(L,d+1)=L(B(L,d)+1),
\]
\[
 R_i=4i(i+2),
\]
\[
 L_i=2\bigl((2R_{i+1}+1)i(i+1)+2R_{i+1}\bigr)+4(i+1)+10,
\]
tends to infinity, but no graph of infinite chromatic number can have every \(n\)-vertex subgraph made bipartite by deleting at most \(f(n)\) edges.
